flaw.answer: `result[^1] = (start, cur.End)` should be `Math.Max(result[^1].End, cur.End)`. **[1,10] + [2,3] becomes [1,3]** — a contained interval shrinks the cover.
flaw.fix: Take the max of the two ends.

qa.a: Red-black tree: O(log n) insert, remove, lookup; in-order enumeration.

qa.q: How do you get a floor (largest ≤ x)?
qa.a: `GetViewBetween(min, x).Max` — O(log n). There is no `floorKey` like Java's TreeMap.

Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: A class that accepts intervals one at a time, merges overlaps, and answers questions about coverage. You choose the bookkeeping.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- `Add(start, end)` merges with anything it overlaps or touches
- `Remove(start, end)` — may split an interval in two
- `Contains(point)`, `CoveredLength`
- State the convention: half-open [start, end)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: "Sort then merge" is for a batch. For a stream you want a sorted structure with a **floor lookup** — the interval starting at or before x — because only the floor and the intervals starting inside the new one can overlap it. That makes Add O(log n + k), and each interval is absorbed once, so amortised O(log n).

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: `SortedSet<(Start, End)>` ordered by start; intervals kept disjoint and non-touching. `GetViewBetween(min, (x,_)).Max` is the floor. `CoveredLength` maintained on every change.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Add: if floor reaches start, absorb it. Absorb every interval starting in [start, end]. Insert the union.
- Remove: collect the floor (if it reaches in) and every interval starting in [start, end); remove each; re-add the left and right remnants.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| SortedSet<(int,int)> + custom comparer | Ordered, O(log n) insert/remove, range views; .NET has no TreeMap.floorKey, this is the idiom |
| long CoveredLength | Maintained incrementally, so reading it is O(1) |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- Add: if floor reaches start, absorb it. Absorb every interval starting in [start, end]. Insert the union.
- Remove: collect the floor (if it reaches in) and every interval starting in [start, end); remove each; re-add the left and right remnants.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: Add/Remove amortised O(log n); Contains O(log n); CoveredLength O(1). Memory O(n).

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- [1,3) + [5,7) + [3,5) → one interval: touching merges under half-open.
- Contained add changes nothing.
- Remove [3,4) from [1,7) splits into two.
- 7 is not in [1,7).
- **Property test**: 300 random trials of 25 add/remove operations against a 60-cell bitmap — coverage, membership and disjointness all match.

learn.title: 10 · Tests
learn.md:
**S1 — Add intervals, keep them merged**

- two intervals
- touching merges to one
- covered
- contained changes nothing
- 3 contained
- 7 not contained (half-open)
- empty interval rejected
- one add absorbs three
- absorbed span
- matches a bitmap over 300 random trials; disjoint and non-touching
- 200,000 disjoint adds in … ms (< 3000 — not O(n) per add)

**S2 — Remove a range**

- remove splits
- covered after split
- 3 gone

- add/remove matches a bitmap over 300 random trials

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Tell it the convention: "half-open [start, end); touching intervals merge".
- Ask for Add only, given your SortedSet field and comparer.
- Ask for a property test against a bitmap — then read it, because the oracle must be obviously correct.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe disjoint, non-touching half-open intervals in a SortedSet keyed by start, with a floor lookup via GetViewBetween(...).Max, so Add is O(log n + k) and amortised O(log n). Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Add, Remove and Contains concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Add Remove(start, end). Removing from the middle splits an interval in two. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- `List` + `Sort` on every insert: O(n log n) per Add.
- Merging with `last.End = cur.End` instead of `Math.Max` — loses containment (R4).
- Closed vs half-open mismatch: [1,2] and [2,3] merge or not.
- Forgetting the floor interval that starts before the new one but reaches into it.

**Verification exercise:** Incorrect logic — `result[^1] = (start, cur.End)` should be `Math.Max(result[^1].End, cur.End)`. **[1,10] + [2,3] becomes [1,3]** — a contained interval shrinks the cover.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
A merge removes several entries and inserts one; a concurrent reader can see the gap. One lock per operation; CoveredLength updated inside it.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Concurrent writers and readers.* — One lock per op; volatile snapshot for CoveredLength

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *Millions of intervals, range-sum queries.* — Segment tree over compressed coordinates

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Integer overflow on `end - start` with large coordinates: use long.
- Inverted or empty intervals: reject or ignore — decide and test it.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *How do you test it in CI?* — Property test vs a bitmap oracle

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Add with merging.* — Floor + range view. Say half-open.
- *Remove.* — Splits. Remnants re-added.
- *Covered length fast.* — Maintain it on every change.
- *Millions of intervals.* — Still log n. If memory is the issue, coarsen; if queries are range sums, a segment tree over compressed coordinates.
- *Concurrent writers.* — One lock (a merge touches several entries). Readers that only need CoveredLength can read a volatile snapshot.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Touching intervals? Inverted? Duplicate add?* — Half-open → touching merges; reject inverted; idempotent

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Brute force vs this?* — Re-sort list O(n log n) per add vs O(log n) amortised
- *Very large N?* — Still log n; memory is the limit

aiGuide.intro: An interval set that stays merged as you add — and later remove — ranges. Assistants reach for the LeetCode "sort and merge" function, which is the wrong shape for a live structure.
plan: Ask: half-open or closed? do touching intervals merge? what is reported?
Invariant + structure: sorted map start → end, floor lookup, running total

stages.name: Add, keep merged
stages.yours: Half-open `[start, end)`. Invariant: **sorted, disjoint, never touching** — `[1,3) + [3,5)` merge. Structure: `SortedList<int,int>` start → end, a binary-search floor lookup, and a running `_covered` total.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** Add, then let the AI write a **property test against a bitmap** — the strongest test for this question.
bad: The LeetCode function: sort a list, merge neighbours, return a new list — O(n log n) on every Add. Often with the R4 bug: `[1,10] + [2,3]` becomes `[1,3]`.
Wrong shape: a function, not a structure
No touching rule, no half-open rule
good: Implement Add(start, end) in IntervalSet below. Half-open [start, end); start >= end throws ArgumentException. Keep my SortedList<int,int> (start → end) sorted, disjoint and non-touching: find the interval at or before start with a binary search, then absorb every interval that overlaps or touches. Update _covered as you go. O(log n + intervals absorbed), no re-sort. State your assumptions first. Show only Add and its helper.
stages.reply: Typical defect (verified planted flaw R4): the merged end set to the absorbed interval's end instead of the **max** — a contained interval **shrinks** the cover.
stages.say: "Touching intervals merge because the ranges are half-open. And I test against a bitmap, so I am not trusting my own examples."
stages.say_iv: I will call addInterval with ranges one at a time. Keep them merged, and let me ask how much is covered and whether a point is covered. Choose the data structure yourself.

stages.name: Remove a range
stages.yours: Say the hard case: **a remove can split one interval into two**. For every overlapping interval: take it out, put back the part left of the cut and the part right of it.
stages.ai: **Co-generate**, and re-run the bitmap property test with removes mixed in.
bad: Removes every interval that overlaps the range — never splits. `[1,7)` minus `[3,4)` removes everything.
The split case is not mentioned, so it is missed
good: Implement Remove(start, end): for every interval overlapping [start, end), take it out and put back the part before start and the part after end, if non-empty. Keep _covered right. Collect the pieces first; do not insert while walking the list by index. Keep my fields and Add unchanged. No re-sort. Explain how _covered stays right. Show only Remove.
stages.reply: Typical defect: inserting the right-hand piece while walking forward by index, which **skips the next interval**.
validate: Remove from the middle splits one interval into two
Remove [7,9) from [1,7): touching, so nothing changes
Property test with mixed add/remove matches a bitmap
stages.fix: Collect-then-insert is a few lines → **a narrow follow-up**: "Collect the leftover pieces in a list and add them after the loop."
stages.say: "A remove can split, so I collect the leftover pieces and add them after the walk."
stages.require: Add `Remove(start, end)`. Removing from the middle splits an interval in two.
